methodological_rigor.justification: Rigorous preclinical design including a 1,166-gene CRISPR-Cas9 dropout screen across three PDX-derived PATC lines, sgRNA-resistant GFER rescue experiments (Fig. 1H–J), orthogonal validation via both anti-CD8 antibody depletion and CD8−/− mice (Fig. 4K, Supplementary Fig. S11A), pharmacologic rescue with H-151, exogenous GSH, and MitoQ, and use of an immunocompetent orthotopic KPC syngeneic model. Weaknesses include: tumor implantation and measurement explicitly not blinded; in vivo RNA-seq relies on very small groups after post-hoc outlier exclusion (n=2 shCTRL, n=3 shGFER#4, n=2 shGFER#5), which is methodologically concerning; the PRINCE cohort analysis uses only n=17 patients; no formal power calculation reported (sample size justified by 'reported literature records' and 'previous outcomes'). Statistical treatment is adequate but basic — two-tailed t-tests and one-way ANOVA with DESeq2 adjusted P<0.05 for RNA-seq — but lacks explicit multiplicity correction across many parallel comparisons, no effect sizes with CIs, and no sensitivity analyses for the post-hoc QC exclusions in the in vivo RNA-seq cohort.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a mechanistic preclinical study using cell lines, PDX xenografts, syngeneic KPC immunocompetent mouse models, and a small retrospective human cohort analysis — Oxford LoE 5 (preclinical/mechanistic). Clinical relevance is nonetheless substantial because PDAC remains refractory to immune checkpoint blockade (5-year survival ~8%) and the paper identifies a novel target that mechanistically converts a cold tumor to one responsive to anti–PD-1 therapy, with correlative human evidence from TCGA and the PRINCE immunotherapy trial (Fig. 4M). The translational path is plausible but preliminary: no GFER-targeting pharmacological agent is tested, only genetic depletion, so first-in-human development remains distant.

reporting_quality.justification: ARRIVE applies as this is a preclinical animal study with substantial in vivo work (PDX, orthotopic KPC, CD8 KO mice, immune checkpoint blockade, STING antagonist studies). Reporting strengths: IACUC approval cited, housing conditions documented (temperature, humidity, photoperiod), euthanasia criteria, randomization of mice to treatment groups, acknowledgment that tumor implantation/measurement were not blinded while IF staining was blinded. Gaps include: no explicit ARRIVE checklist, limited reporting of exact animal numbers used vs excluded, no detailed sample size justification beyond 'reported literature,' post-hoc exclusion of RNA-seq outliers reported but not pre-specified. Data/code availability is not described in the retained text — no accession numbers for RNA-seq data, no code repository, cell line and reagent catalog numbers are well documented but underlying raw data location is not stated.

novelty_literature.justification: The identification of GFER as a dual-function target in PDAC — simultaneously regulating mitochondrial redox homeostasis and tumor immunogenicity via the CHAC1–GSH–mtDNA–cGAS-STING axis — is genuinely novel in this tumor type; prior GFER literature focused on hepatocarcinoma and liver fibrosis (refs 26, 27, 32). The mechanistic link between mitochondrial redox perturbation and cGAS-STING activation has precedent (e.g., Mangalhara et al. 2023 in melanoma, ref 22), so the overarching framework is incremental, but applying it through a novel upstream node (GFER) in the uniquely immunosuppressive PDAC TME, combined with ICB sensitization data, represents a meaningful extension. Novelty falls primarily in the empirical/mechanistic dimension rather than first-in-class discovery.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with a clear narrative arc from CRISPR screen → target validation → mechanism (redox/CHAC1/GSH) → immunomodulation (cGAS-STING, CD8+ T cells) → therapeutic combination with anti–PD-1. The abstract is quantitatively grounded and accurately previews the findings. Figure captions are detailed and standalone-interpretable with explicit statistical tests, n values, and cell numbers. Minor issues: some grammatical awkwardness (e.g., 'daily treated with vehicle,' 'divided in to GFER-high'), occasional redundancy in abstract (two near-identical opening sentences), and the single-sentence hedging statement in Results about GFER tolerability in normal cells reads unpolished.

key_strengths: Unbiased CRISPR screen with functional validation across multiple PDX models and orthogonal rescue (sgRNA-resistant GFER) establishes target credibility
Mechanistic chain is coherent and pharmacologically interrogated: redox perturbation → mtDNA cytosolic release → cGAS-STING → type I IFN → CD8+ T-cell infiltration, with H-151, GSH, and MitoQ rescues
Dual orthogonal in vivo validation of CD8+ T-cell dependence using both anti-CD8 antibody depletion and CD8−/− mice
Translationally relevant combination with anti–PD-1 in immunocompetent KPC syngeneic model with supportive human correlative data from TCGA and PRINCE trial
Addresses a major unmet need (ICB resistance in PDAC) with a mechanistically novel target
key_concerns: In vivo RNA-seq uses very small group sizes (n=2, 3, 2) after post-hoc outlier exclusion, undermining confidence in differential expression findings
PRINCE immunotherapy correlation is based on only n=17 patients and should be presented as hypothesis-generating rather than supportive
No pharmacological GFER inhibitor is tested; translational claims rely entirely on genetic depletion with no druggability demonstration
No power calculation or formal effect-size reporting with CIs; multiplicity correction limited to DESeq2
Data/code availability not stated in retained manuscript; no RNA-seq accession number visible
Tumor measurement not blinded (acknowledged); senescence induction and chemotherapy resistance implications warrant deeper discussion
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid preclinical mechanistic study with coherent target identification, mechanism, and in vivo ICB combination data, well-suited to a Tier 2 oncology journal (e.g., JECCR/JITC/Molecular Cancer-adjacent); not quite paradigm-shifting enough for Tier 1 given reliance on genetic rather than pharmacologic GFER inhibition and small-cohort correlative human data. Minor revisions should strengthen reporting of in vivo RNA-seq sample sizes/exclusions, add data availability, and temper claims from the n=17 PRINCE analysis.
